paras: The whipping of Moses M. Dempster was a mob beating of a Black man near Monticello, Mississippi, reported under a June 1, 1919, dateline. Accused of shooting at a bill collector, Dempster was taken into the woods by armed men and beaten with a buggy trace, and the report credited a sheriff's plea for "the whip instead of the rope" with saving his life.

According to the dispatch, a bill collector named in the text as Holmes went to Dempster's home to collect a bill. Dempster "was said to have been impudent," and Holmes raised a heavy stick to strike "the colored man." The following sentences are garbled in the surviving text, but they indicate that Dempster, frightened, fired at the collector, who then retreated.

For the shooting, Dempster was taken into the woods by men armed with a rifle and shotguns. The report said that "only the earnest plea of the sheriff to use the whip instead of the rope saved his life," implying that the men had meant to hang him. Instead he was beaten with a buggy trace, a beating the paper described with a word printed as "unnecessitely."
The brief names none of the men and gives no race for them or for the collector, and no report of an arrest, charge or inquiry appears in the coverage.

The only report found ran on the front page of the Baltimore Afro-American on June 13, 1919, as an unheadlined paragraph between an item on a Baltimore church fund drive and a Washington note on Emmett J. Scott's resignation. The Afro-American's version put the collector's raised stick before Dempster's shot and presented the whipping as a lynching narrowly averted. No other Black newspaper in the coverage carried the story, and no editorial comment on it was found.

reader.title: Whipping of Moses M. Dempster
bases: Armed men took Dempster into the woods and beat him with a buggy trace; the sheriff's plea for 'the whip instead of the rope' indicates a hanging was contemplated but he was whipped and survived (A2).

Dempster was beaten but not killed, so the standard definition is not met; the brief presents it as a lynching averted by the sheriff's plea, carried out without legal authority in punishment for an alleged shooting at a bill collector (A2).
Only one report, a short dated brief in the Baltimore Afro-American, was found (A2).

accounts.label: Monticello dispatch in the Black press
accounts.gist: Dempster, said to have been impudent to a bill collector who raised a stick to hit him, shot at the collector; armed men took him to the woods, and on the sheriff's plea he was whipped with a buggy trace rather than hanged.

framing.detail: The brief, run without a headline among unrelated news, stresses that the collector raised his stick first and that Dempster was beaten 'unnecessitely' [unmercifully?], with his life saved only by the sheriff's plea.
